Look‑alike conditions: drug‑induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide), mixed connective tissue disease, dermatomyositis, infection‑related vasculitis.

qs.q: Who was the dermatologist credited with first describing dermatomyositis in 1891?
qs.e: Dermatomyositis was first described by the dermatologist Unna in 1891. Bohan and Peter are associated with the classification criteria.

qs.q: Which cutaneous manifestation is specifically associated with dermatomyositis, presenting on the eyelids?
qs.e: Dermatomyositis is associated with a characteristic heliotrope rash on the eyelids. A malar butterfly rash is classically seen in systemic lupus erythematosus rather than dermatomyositis.

qs.q: A patient with dermatomyositis is evaluated for respiratory involvement. Aside from pulmonary fibrosis and bronchial carcinoma, what structural component is characteristically affected in the airways and chest wall?
qs.e: Dermatomyositis and polymyositis characteristically involve intercostal and diaphragmatic myopathy. Esophageal disease leading to aspiration pneumonia is a feature of systemic sclerosis.

ai.title: Dermatomyositis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Dermatomyositis is an immune-mediated inflammatory myopathy with characteristic skin findings and proximal muscle weakness. Diagnosis relies on clinical features, muscle enzymes, autoantibodies and muscle biopsy. Management combines immunosuppression, supportive care and cancer screening.

sections.p: Dermatomyositis (DM) is a systemic autoimmune disease causing inflammation of skeletal muscle and skin. It belongs to the idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM).
b: Bohan and Peter criteria (1975) – requires 3 of 5: typical rash, symmetric proximal weakness, elevated CK, EMG changes, muscle biopsy with perifascicular atrophy.
2017 EULAR/ACR classification – uses a weighted score of age, rash, muscle weakness, CK, autoantibodies, and biopsy.

sections.p: Severity is graded by muscle strength (Medical Research Council scale) and extent of extramuscular disease (lung, heart, malignancy).
b: Mild: MRC grade ≥4/5, CK <5× upper limit, no organ involvement.
Moderate: MRC 3–4, CK 5–10× ULN, interstitial lung disease (ILD) possible.
Severe: MRC ≤2, CK >10× ULN, ILD, cardiac involvement, or malignancy.

sections.p: DM is idiopathic but driven by autoimmunity; several triggers are recognised, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Autoantibodies (anti‑Mi‑2, anti‑MDA5, anti‑TIF1‑γ) – most common intrinsic cause.
Infections prevalent in East Africa – HIV, hepatitis B, TB, malaria can precipitate or mimic DM.
Paraneoplastic – nasopharyngeal carcinoma, cervical cancer, Kaposi sarcoma are more common locally.
Drug‑induced – statins, hydroxychloroquine, herbal remedies containing heavy metals.

sections.p: Patients present with a combination of skin and muscle findings that develop over weeks to months.
b: Heliotrope rash – violaceous discoloration of eyelids, often with swelling.
Gottron papules – raised, scaly erythematous lesions over knuckles, elbows, knees.
Symmetric proximal weakness – difficulty rising, climbing stairs, lifting objects.
Painful muscle cramps, fatigue, dysphagia if pharyngeal muscles involved.
Systemic features – low‑grade fever, arthralgia, Raynaud’s phenomenon.

sections.p: If a test is unavailable (e.g., EMG), rely on clinical pattern, CK, ANA and consider referral for biopsy when possible.

t.b: Is there active muscle injury? – Elevated >5× upper limit confirms myositis; normal does not exclude disease.

t.a: ANA and myositis‑specific antibodies (Mi‑2, MDA5, TIF1‑γ)
t.b: What is the immunologic profile? – Positive antibodies support DM and may hint at cancer risk.
Does the muscle show myopathic changes? – Short, polyphasic motor units and fibrillation potentials indicate inflammation.
Gold standard for diagnosis when other data are equivocal – shows characteristic histology.
Is interstitial lung disease present? – Ground‑glass opacities suggest ILD, a major cause of mortality.

t.a: Cancer screening (age‑appropriate ultrasound, pap smear, HPV testing)
t.b: Is there an underlying malignancy? – Detects paraneoplastic DM, especially nasopharyngeal or cervical cancer.
Are infections a trigger? – Positive results guide additional treatment and infection control.

sections.p: Complications drive mortality and dictate urgent actions.
b: Rapidly progressive interstitial lung disease – dyspnoea, hypoxia.
Cardiac involvement – arrhythmias, myocarditis, heart failure.
Dysphagia leading to aspiration pneumonia.
Malignancy – especially nasopharyngeal, cervical, ovarian cancers.
Severe skin ulceration or calcinosis causing infection.

sections.p: Treat the autoimmune process, protect organs, and address triggers.
b: First‑line: High‑dose oral prednisone (or IV methylprednisolone if severe) – rapidly suppresses inflammation.
Steroid‑sparing agents: Azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil – chosen for oral use, lower infection risk than cyclophosphamide.
IVIG – useful when refractory or when infection limits steroid use.
Avoid long‑term cyclophosphamide unless life‑threatening ILD, due to bone‑marrow toxicity.
Physiotherapy – early gentle range‑of‑motion to prevent contractures.
Skin care – sunscreen, topical steroids for rash, wound care for ulcerations.
Cancer surveillance – repeat screening every 6‑12 months for 5 years.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects relapse, drug toxicity and emerging complications.
b: Clinic review every 4–6 weeks until stable, then every 3–6 months.
CK and liver function tests at each visit; adjust immunosuppression accordingly.
Pulmonary function tests annually or sooner if dyspnoea.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus; avoid live vaccines while on high‑dose steroids.
Educate patients on early signs of infection, dysphagia and skin ulceration.

sections.p: Several conditions share rash or muscle weakness.
b: Polymyositis – lacks characteristic skin findings; CD8+ endomysial infiltrates on biopsy.
Systemic lupus erythematosus – malar rash, but usually ANA high with dsDNA, and renal involvement.
Drug‑induced lupus – history of hydralazine or procainamide, antihistone antibodies.
Infection‑related vasculitis – fever, purpura, often with positive blood cultures.

sections.p: Certain labs may be normal despite active disease.
b: CK can be normal in early DM or in patients on chronic steroids; rely on clinical exam and EMG.
ANA may be negative; myositis‑specific antibodies are more informative.
Chest X‑ray may miss early ILD; HRCT is required if symptoms suggest lung disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening dyspnoea or hypoxia (possible ILD flare)
Severe dysphagia with weight loss or aspiration
New chest pain or palpitations (cardiac involvement)
Rapidly expanding skin ulcer or necrosis

faq.q: Why is a skin rash essential for diagnosing dermatomyositis?
faq.a: The heliotrope rash and Gottron papules are highly specific and differentiate DM from polymyositis.

faq.q: Can CK be normal in dermatomyositis?
faq.a: Yes, especially early or when steroids blunt the enzyme rise; clinical assessment remains crucial.

faq.q: What is the most important cancer screening in East African patients with DM?
faq.a: Nasopharyngeal and cervical cancer screening, because these are relatively common malignancies linked to DM in the region.

exam: A 25‑year‑old woman presents with heliotrope rash and proximal weakness. Which diagnostic criteria do you apply first and why? — Use Bohan and Peter; need rash + weakness + CK or EMG.
Your patient’s CK is normal but muscle strength is 2/5 proximally. How do you proceed? — Trust clinical exam; obtain EMG or biopsy, consider early steroids.
A DM patient develops new dry cough and fine crackles. What is your next step? — Order HRCT to assess ILD; start high‑dose steroids if ILD confirmed.
Which immunosuppressive drug would you add if the patient cannot taper steroids due to side effects? — Choose azathioprine or methotrexate; explain rationale and monitoring.
How does anti‑MDA5 antibody status influence management? — Associated with rapidly progressive ILD; warrants aggressive immunosuppression and close pulmonary monitoring.

A patient on long‑term steroids for DM presents with fever and neutropenia. What is your immediate action? — Stop steroids, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, evaluate for infection before increasing immunosuppression.
What distinguishes dermatomyositis from polymyositis on muscle biopsy? — Perifascicular atrophy with CD4+ perivascular infiltrates vs. endomysial CD8+ infiltrates.
Why is cancer screening mandatory in newly diagnosed DM, and how often should it be repeated? — Up to 30% have occult malignancy; repeat every 6–12 months for 5 years.
